The Temple in Jerusalem refers to successive sanctuaries built on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem that served as the primary center of Israelite and Jewish worship, sacrifice, and national identity. The First Temple, built by King Solomon, was destroyed by the Babylonians in five hundred eighty-six BC. The Second Temple, reconstructed under Zerubbabel and later heavily renovated by Herod the Great, was destroyed by the Romans in seventy AD, leaving only the Western Wall standing and initiating the transition to rabbinic Judaism.

The First Temple was constructed by King Solomon in the tenth century BC on Mount Moriah. It housed the Ark of the Covenant in its innermost sanctuary, the Holy of Holies. The First Temple was sacked and completely destroyed by the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II in five hundred eighty-six BC, sending the Jewish people into the Babylonian Exile.

The Second Temple was constructed on the same site after Cyrus the Great authorized the return of Jewish exiles. It was later massively expanded by Herod the Great to become one of the grandest structures of the Roman East. In the second century BC, the Hellenistic king Antiochus IV Epiphanes desecrated the Second Temple by dedicating it to Zeus, sparking the Maccabean Revolt and leading to the temple's rededication, commemorated by the holiday of Hanukkah.

The Second Temple was destroyed by Roman legions under the future emperor Titus in seventy AD during the First Jewish-Roman War, an event mourned annually on the fast of Tisha B'Av. The innermost chamber, the Holy of Holies, was entered only once a year by the High Priest on Yom Kippur, separated from the rest of the temple by a heavy veil. The Gospels record that this veil split in two at the moment of Jesus's crucifixion.
